claim: The sample included 60,159 supporting findings and 4253 opposing findings about 51,292 drug-gene interaction claims in 3363 scientific articles.
source: Our sample included 60,159 supporting findings and 4253 opposing findings about 51,292 drug-gene interaction claims in 3363 scientific articles.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 1A and the methods section describing the CTD and LINCS L1000 data matching.

claim: Claims reported in a single paper replicate 19.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 16.9–21.2%) more frequently than expected.
source: We show that claims reported in a single paper replicate 19.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 16.9–21.2%) more frequently than expected
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis presented in the abstract and detailed in Figure 2E showing relative replication increase for Low support claims.

claim: Claims reported in multiple papers replicate 45.5% (95% CI, 21.8–74.2%) more frequently than expected.
source: while claims reported in multiple papers replicate 45.5% (95% CI, 21.8–74.2%) more frequently than expected.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis presented in the abstract and detailed in Figure 2E showing relative replication increase for Very High support claims.

claim: Centralized scientific communities propagate less replicable claims than decentralized communities.
source: We also analyze the subsample of interactions with two or more published findings (2493 claims; 6272 supporting findings; 339 opposing findings; 1282 research articles), and show that centralized scientific communities, which use similar methods and involve shared authors who contribute to many articles, propagate less replicable claims than decentralized communities, which use more diverse methods and contain more independent teams.
evidence: This is supported by the logistic regression analysis in Figure 4A showing that centralization has an odds ratio of 0.36 (95% CI, 0.27–0.48) for replication success.

claim: The CTD had recorded over 1.26 million drug-gene interaction (DGI) claims published in journals as of June 7, 2016.
source: The CTD had recorded over 1.26 million drug-gene interaction (DGI) claims published in journals as of June 7, 2016
evidence: This is a factual statement about the database size at a specific date, presented in the Results section.

claim: The LINCS L1000 experiment generated 1.3 million gene expression profiles from 42,080 perturbagens across a range of different cell lines, time points and dosage levels.
source: The LINCS L1000 experiment generated 1.3 million gene expression profiles from 42,080 perturbagens across a range of different cell lines, time points and dosage levels.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the LINCS L1000 dataset, supported by citation to Subramanian et al., 2017.

claim: Most claims (89%) are supported by findings in one or two (8%) articles.
source: Most claims are supported by findings in one (89%) or two (8%) articles, while few appear in many articles.
evidence: This is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The vast majority of published findings (93%) agree on the direction of DGI claims.
source: There is wide consensus in the literature: the vast majority of published findings (93%) agree on the direction of DGI claims.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of agreement in the literature.

claim: Among claims supported by two or more published findings, the agreement increases to 94%.
source: Among the 11% of claims supported by two or more published findings, the agreement increases to 94%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of agreement in the literature for multi-study claims.

claim: Only 41% (21,181/51,292) of the DGI effect-sizes in LINCS L1000 generalize across experimental conditions.
source: In contrast, only 41% (21,181/51,292) of the DGI effect-sizes in LINCS L1000 generalize across experimental conditions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the LINCS L1000 data analysis, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A pair of findings about a DGI claim reported in papers with some of the same authors are significantly more likely to agree (0.989) than findings reported in papers by socially independent teams (0.889).
source: Further, we find that consensus in the biomedical literature is strongly and positively associated with connections between papers arising from overlapping authors. A pair of findings about a DGI claim reported in papers with some of the same authors are significantly more likely to agree (0.989, 2486 of 2514 overlapping pairs of papers) than findings reported in papers by socially independent teams (0.889, 18,527 of 20,846 non-overlapping pairs of papers), with a mean difference of 0.1001 (95% CI, 0.094–0.106, P <.0001, 100,000 bootstrap iterations; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage relative replication increase (RRI) for the entire sample is 10.6% (95% CI, 9.3%–11.8%).
source: this corresponds to a per centage relative replication increase (RRI = ((RRobs – RRrand)/RRrand) × 100%) of 10.6% (95% CI, 9.3%–11.8%).
evidence: This is calculated from the observed and random replication rates.

claim: Claims with Very High support in the biomedical literature replicate 45.5% (95% CI, 21.8–74.2%) more frequently than expected.
source: Figure 2E shows that claims with Very High support in the biomedical literature (RRI = 45.5%; 95% CI, 21.8–74.2%) with an average of 6.9 papers confirming the claim
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E for the Very High support category.

claim: Claims with High support replicate 34.5% (95% CI, 20.2–50.3%) more frequently than expected.
source: and claims with High support (RRI = 34.5%; 20.2–50.3%) with an average of 3.3 confirming papers
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E for the High support category.

claim: Claims with Low support replicate 19.0% (95% CI, 16.9–21.2%) more frequently than expected.
source: are substantially more likely to replicate in high-throughput experiments than those with Low and Moderate support (RRI = 19.0%; 16.9–21.2% and 16.2%; 9.8–22.9%, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E for the Low support category.

claim: Claims with Moderate support replicate 16.2% (95% CI, 9.8–22.9%) more frequently than expected.
source: are substantially more likely to replicate in high-throughput experiments than those with Low and Moderate support (RRI = 19.0%; 16.9–21.2% and 16.2%; 9.8–22.9%, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E for the Moderate support category.

claim: Not Supported claims are significantly less likely to replicate than random (RRI = −28.9%; −61.9%–16.7%).
source: whereas Not Supported claims are significantly less likely to replicate than random (RRI = −28.9%; −61.9%–16.7%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E for the Not Supported category.

claim: Not Supported claims are associated with greater experimental variability.
source: They are also associated with greater experimental variability (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F comparing variability across support categories.

claim: The replication of claims with Low and Moderate support is consistent with reproducibility estimates reported in the literature, ranging from 11% (N = 67; Begley and Ellis, 2012) to 25% (N = 53; Prinz et al., 2011).
source: The replication of claims with Low and Moderate support is consistent with reproducibility estimates reported in the literature, ranging from 11% (N = 67; Begley and Ellis, 2012) to 25% (N = 53; Prinz et al., 2011).
evidence: This compares the findings to prior published reproducibility studies.

claim: The majority of claims (89%) in the corpus are only reported in a single paper.
source: We note that the process of collective correction applies to a small subset of claims as the majority of claims (89%) in our corpus are only reported in a single paper.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the distribution analysis.

claim: Single-study claims have an observed replication rate (RRobs) of only 0.601.
source: This interpretation is supported by our finding that single-study claims in our corpus (ie, claims in the Low support class) have a RRobs of only 0.601
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the replication analysis of single-study claims.

claim: The first published studies about multiple-studied claims that eventually achieve High or Very High support have an observed replication rate (RRobs) of 0.720.
source: while the first published studies about multiple-studied claims that eventually achieve High or Very High support have a RRobs of 0.720.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the replication analysis of first studies in multi-study claims.

claim: The subsample for network dependency analysis consists of 2493 claims, associated with 6272 supporting and 339 opposing findings from 1282 research articles.
source: The resulting subsample consists of 2493 claims, associated with 6272 supporting and 339 opposing findings from 1282 research articles (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the subsample used for the network analysis.

claim: When all predictors are modeled simultaneously, centralization and support in the literature largely account for all of the other predictors.
source: When all predictors are modeled simultaneously (Figure 4A), centralization and support in the literature largely account for all of the others.
evidence: This is from the multivariate logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Centralized and extensive biomedical collaboration is associated with use of the same biomedical research techniques and attention to the same prior research.
source: This suggests that centralized and extensive biomedical collaboration is associated with use of the same biomedical research techniques and attention to the same prior research (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Claims originally reported and subsequently confirmed by papers with overlapping authors resulted in much more centralized communities (mean C = 0.6164; 95% CI, 0.5925–0.6402) compared to claims reported and subsequently confirmed by papers with independent authors (mean C = 0.4004; 95% CI, 0.3765–0.4242).
source: Focusing on High and Very High support claims with some degree of centralization (n = 295), we found that claims originally reported and subsequently confirmed by papers with overlapping authors (n = 117) resulted in much more centralized communities (mean C = 0.6164; 95% CI, 0.5925–0.6402) compared to claims reported and subsequently confirmed by papers with independent authors (n = 178; mean C = 0.4004; 95% CI, 0.3765–0.4242; two-way ANOVA test with unbalanced design.)
evidence: This is from an exploratory analysis comparing centralization for claims with and without author overlap.

claim: Claim replication increases with journal prominence.
source: Claim replication increases with journal prominence (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is from the logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Claims supported by many publications have about 45% higher predicted probability to replicate when investigated by decentralized versus centralized communities.
source: Figure 4B shows that by accounting for biomedical support and decentralization, we can identify claims with high predicted probability of replication. Claims supported by many publications have about 45% higher predicted probability to replicate when investigated by decentralized versus centralized communities.
evidence: This is from the interaction model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: If a DGI claim garners wide support but is studied exclusively by a centralized scientific community, the claim has a predicted probability of replication that is similar to that for a claim reported in a single paper.
source: Even if a DGI claim garners wide support, if it is studied exclusively by a centralized scientific community, the claim has a predicted probability of replication that is similar to that for a claim reported in a single paper.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Claims robust to many, socially independent investigations have 55% higher predicted probability of replication than those studied by a few overlapping collaborations.
source: Likewise, claims robust to many, socially independent investigations have 55% higher predicted probability of replication than those studied by a few overlapping collaborations (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is from the interaction model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The LINCS L1000 data have been reported to be highly reproducible compared to drug screen data generated via RNA sequencing.
source: The LINCS L1000 data have been reported to be highly reproducible (Subramanian et al., 2017) compared to drug screen data generated via RNA sequencing, instances of which have been found to exhibit inconsistencies across platforms (Haibe-Kains et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Subramanian et al., 2017 and Haibe-Kains et al., 2013.

claim: A search in PubMed identified no reference to the LINCS L1000 data among the 3363 articles in the corpus.
source: To verify that published findings have been obtained independently from the LINCS L1000 high-throughput data, a search in PubMed was performed using the search terms LINCS L1000 and L1000. The search identified no reference to the LINCS L1000 data among the 3363 articles.
evidence: This is a verification step to ensure independence between the literature and LINCS L1000 data.

claim: Replication failures are typically attributed to systemic bias in a publication system that favors positive results.
source: Replication failures are typically attributed to systemic bias in a publication system that favors positive results (Ioannidis, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature on replication failures, supported by citation to Ioannidis, 2005.

claim: Publication bias incentivizes questionable research choices such as p-hacking, 'flexible' data analysis, low statistical power, selective reporting, and confirmation bias.
source: This incentivizes questionable research choices such as p-hacking (Head et al., 2015; Simonsohn et al., 2014), 'flexible' data analysis (Simmons et al., 2011), low statistical power (Dumas-Mallet et al., 2017), selective reporting (the 'file drawer problem') (Rosenthal, 1979), and confirmation bias (Nuzzo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature on questionable research practices.

claim: A decentralized community of largely independent, non-overlapping teams, which draws from a diverse pool of prior publications, using distinct methods under varying experimental conditions, is more likely to produce robust results.
source: We hypothesize that a decentralized community of largely independent, non-overlapping teams, which draws from a diverse pool of prior publications, using distinct methods under varying experimental conditions, is more likely to produce robust results.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper, tested through the empirical analysis.

claim: A centralized community involving repeated collaborations and using a narrow range of methods, knowledge from prior publications and experimental conditions is likely to produce less robust results.
source: Conversely, we expect that a centralized community involving repeated collaborations and using a narrow range of methods, knowledge from prior publications and experimental conditions is likely to produce less robust results.
evidence: This is the contrasting hypothesis of the paper, tested through the empirical analysis.

claim: Repeated collaboration, growing teams, star scientists, expensive shared equipment, and common citations are defining characteristics of the biomedical research enterprise today.
source: Unfortunately, repeated collaboration (Hicks and Katz, 1996; Guimerà et al., 2005), growing teams (Wuchty et al., 2007), star scientists (Merton, 1968; Azoulay et al., 2014), expensive shared equipment, and common citations (Evans, 2008; Simkin and Roychowdhury, 2005; White et al., 2004) are defining characteristics of the biomedical research enterprise today (Hicks and Katz, 1996; Hand, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature on scientific collaboration and organization.

claim: Prior simulations have suggested that independent labs are less prone to peer pressure than a densely connected network of scientists, in which misleading early results can propagate more easily.
source: Prior simulations have suggested that independent labs are less prone to peer pressure than a densely connected network of scientists, in which misleading early results can propagate more easily (Zollman, 2007; Payette, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to simulation studies by Zollman, 2007 and Payette, 2012.

claim: Research on the 'wisdom of crowds' and the exploration-exploitation trade-off found densely connected networks to be inefficient, and suggested that networks of semi-isolated subgroups would lead to an improvement in collective performance.
source: Related research on the 'wisdom of crowds' (Lorenz et al., 2011) and the exploration-exploitation trade-off (Lazer and Friedman, 2007) also found densely connected networks to be inefficient, and suggested that networks of semi-isolated subgroups would lead to an improvement in collective performance (Fang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lorenz et al., 2011, Lazer and Friedman, 2007, and Fang et al., 2010.

claim: In estimation tasks completed by networks of individuals, the dominance of central individuals in networks tended to bias the collective estimation process and decrease the average accuracy of group estimates.
source: A more recent experiment demonstrates that decentralized networks, rather than independence, may most improve collective performance. In estimation tasks completed by networks of individuals, it was found that the dominance of central individuals in networks tended to bias the collective estimation process and decrease the average accuracy of group estimates (Becker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Becker et al., 2017.

claim: A separate body of literature attributes robustness of scientific findings to diverse methods used to corroborate them or distinct theories used to motivate them.
source: A separate body of literature attributes robustness of scientific findings to diverse methods (Kaelin, 2017; Wimsatt, 2012) used to corroborate them or distinct theories used to motivate them.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaelin, 2017 and Wimsatt, 2012.

claim: Jean Perrin used multiple experimental techniques and theories to precisely determine Avogadro's number.
source: A classic example is Jean Perrin's use of multiple experimental techniques and theories to precisely determine Avogadro's number (Salmon, 1984).
evidence: This is a historical example supported by citation to Salmon, 1984.

claim: There has been no comprehensive evaluation of the relationship between the way scientific communities are networked and the robustness and replicability of published findings.
source: Nevertheless, there has been no comprehensive evaluation of the relationship between the way scientific communities are networked and the robustness and replicability of published findings.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this paper addresses.

claim: Literature on research reliability has focused on methodological features rather than the way scientific communities are networked.
source: Similarly, literature on research reliability has focused on methodological features rather than the way scientific communities are networked.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of prior literature.

claim: There has been relatively little research on replication in the field of biomedical science.
source: Moreover, there has been relatively little research of this nature in the field of biomedical science.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this paper addresses.

claim: The overwhelming agreement observed in the literature compared to the LINCS L1000 data suggests that the literature may influence the selection and interpretation of experimental results by scientists through confirmation bias.
source: Although those two quantities – agreement among published findings and generalizability of LINCS L1000 effect sizes – are not directly comparable as they utilize different measurements, the overwhelming agreement observed in the literature compared to the LINCS L1000 data suggests that the literature may influence the selection and interpretation of experimental results by scientists through confirmation bias.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of agreement rates in the literature (93%) versus generalizability in LINCS L1000 (41%).

claim: One consequence of confirmation bias is that experimental results that contradict preexisting knowledge are 'filed away' rather than submitted to journals.
source: One consequence of this is that experimental results that contradict preexisting knowledge are 'filed away' rather than submitted to journals (Rosenthal, 1979).
evidence: This is an inference about the file drawer problem, supported by citation to Rosenthal, 1979.

claim: Some disagreement within the literature is attributable to experimental and biological variation in the experiments performed by different scientists.
source: Encouragingly, this suggests that some disagreement within the literature is attributable to experimental and biological variation in the experiments performed by different scientists.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that generalized LINCS L1000 DGIs have higher replication rates than non-generalized ones.

claim: Social dependencies could impact the composition of researchers studying a claim by discouraging researchers outside the dense communities of researchers who initially lay claim to it from pursuing or reporting their findings.
source: Social dependencies could impact the composition of researchers studying a claim by discouraging researchers outside the dense communities of researchers who initially lay claim to it from pursuing or reporting their findings, as suggested in previous research (Azoulay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to Azoulay et al., 2015.

claim: Claims exhibiting social dependencies very early in their development likely receive limited attention and reportage from researchers outside the communities that originated them.
source: This exploratory result suggests that claims exhibiting social dependencies very early in their development likely receive limited attention and reportage from researchers outside the communities that originated them.
evidence: This is an inference from the exploratory analysis of centralization in claims with early author overlap.

claim: Experimental variability has a negative, marginally significant effect on replication.
source: Figure 4A shows that experimental variability has a negative, marginally significant effect on replication
evidence: This is from the logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Support from multiple teams organized in decentralized communities are much more informative predictors of replication success than experimental variability.
source: but support from multiple teams organized in decentralized communities are much more informative predictors of replication success.
evidence: This is from the comparison of effect sizes in the logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Prominent journals are responsible for only a tiny fraction of all claims.
source: but prominent journals are responsible for only a tiny fraction of all claims.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of journal prominence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Collective correction in science can be undermined when one or several scientists exercise disproportionate influence on research across multiple investigations of a claim.
source: This suggests that collective correction in science can be undermined when one or several scientists exercise disproportionate influence on research across multiple investigations of a claim.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that centralized communities produce less replicable claims.

claim: A claim studied exclusively by a centralized scientific community is unlikely to clear a clinical trial or enter medical practice.
source: It is unlikely that such a claim will clear a clinical trial or enter medical practice (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the low predicted probability of replication for centralized claims.

claim: Research replicability is associated with the way scientific collaborations are networked, after adjusting for variability in high-throughput experiments and the methodology of published studies.
source: It provides evidence that research replicability is associated with the way scientific collaborations are networked, after adjusting for variability in high-throughput experiments and the methodology of published studies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, supported by the multivariate logistic regression analysis.

claim: Centralized, overlapping communities with shared methodologies and exposure to the same prior knowledge are supported by extensive collaboration, ubiquitous communication technologies, a reward system that places a premium on productivity, and cumulative advantage processes that create central, star biomedical scientists.
source: Centralized, overlapping communities with shared methodologies and exposure to the same prior knowledge are supported by extensive collaboration (Hicks and Katz, 1996; Hand, 2010), ubiquitous communication technologies, a reward system that places a premium on productivity, and cumulative advantage processes that create central, star biomedical scientists (Azoulay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on scientific collaboration and organization.

claim: Centralized communities are associated with scientific findings of lower replicability.
source: Our results indicate that such communities are associated with scientific findings of lower replicability.
evidence: This is the main finding of the paper, supported by the logistic regression analysis.

claim: Decentralized, sparsely connected communities explore diverse research methodologies and prior knowledge and are more likely to generate replicable findings.
source: Decentralized, sparsely connected communities explore diverse research methodologies and prior knowledge (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and are more likely to generate replicable findings.
evidence: This is the main finding of the paper, supported by the logistic regression analysis and correlation analysis.

claim: Nissen et al. reason that even if many studies converge on the same finding, this may not increase our confidence because the same systematic biases that made the original finding false are also likely to affect subsequent findings, resulting in a canonization of 'false facts'.
source: Nissen et al. reason that even if many studies converge on the same finding, this may not increase our confidence because the same systematic biases – publication bias in particular – that made the original finding false are also likely to affect subsequent findings, resulting in a canonization of 'false facts' (Nissen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of the argument made by Nissen et al., 2016.

claim: The analysis identifies conditions under which the argument of Nissen et al. holds, namely for research claims studied by centralized, overlapping collaborations.
source: Our analysis identifies conditions under which such an argument holds, namely for research claims studied by centralized, overlapping collaborations.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that centralized communities produce less replicable claims even with multiple studies.

claim: In the absence of social independence, replicability is low and the likelihood of a claim being revised or withdrawn is virtually non-existent as authors and methods reinforce agreement with themselves.
source: In the absence of social independence, replicability is low and the likelihood of a claim being revised or withdrawn is virtually non-existent as authors and methods reinforce agreement with themselves.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings on social independence and centralization.

claim: Both disagreement and replication increase when teams from a decentralized or sparsely connected community provide separate confirming evidence for a claim.
source: Both disagreement and replication increase when teams from a decentralized or sparsely connected community provide separate confirming evidence for a claim.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings on decentralization and social independence.

claim: The findings allay science policy concerns over a universal 'replication crisis' and identify conditions that facilitate collective convergence on replicable findings in biomedical science.
source: Our findings allay science policy concerns over a universal 'replication crisis' and identify conditions – decentralized and novel collaborations – that facilitate collective convergence on replicable findings in biomedical science.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings for science policy.

claim: Certain 'big science' initiatives, such as the human genome project, involve large international consortiums that require a degree of repeated collaboration and centralization by design.
source: We acknowledge that certain 'big science' initiatives (Hand, 2010), such as the human genome project (International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2001), involve large international consortiums that require a degree of repeated collaboration and centralization by design.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of exceptions to the general findings, supported by citations.

claim: The current organization of science incentivizes repeated collaborations.
source: It is also the case that the current organization of science incentivizes repeated collaborations (Guimerà et al., 2005; Lungeanu and Contractor, 2015; Hilton and Cooke, 2015), including centralized communities revolving around star scientists (Azoulay et al., 2014) or prestigious and well-endowed institutes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on scientific collaboration.

claim: By reducing information and coordination costs, repeated collaborations are more productive than new ones.
source: By reducing information and coordination costs, repeated collaborations are more productive than new ones (Hilton and Cooke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hilton and Cooke, 2015.

claim: Projects that involve prior collaborators are more likely to be funded and successfully completed.
source: Consequently, projects that involve prior collaborators are more likely to be funded (Lungeanu et al., 2014) and successfully completed (Cummings and Kiesler, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lungeanu et al., 2014 and Cummings and Kiesler, 2008.

claim: Positive feedback from repeated collaborations can lead to the lock-in of rigid collaborative clusters, which produce voluminous scientific output with diminished value for the wider biomedical field.
source: Such positive feedback, however, can lead to the lock-in of rigid collaborative clusters, which produce voluminous scientific output with diminished value for the wider biomedical field.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings on centralization and productivity.

claim: Science policies supporting biomedicine should account for the trade-off between increased productivity and diminished reliability.
source: Science policies supporting biomedicine should account for the trade-off between increased productivity and diminished reliability.
evidence: This is a policy recommendation based on the findings.

claim: The approach does not rely on the LINCS L1000 data being completely free from error.
source: We note, however, that our approach does not rely on the LINCS L1000 data being completely free from error.
evidence: This is a clarification about the assumptions of the approach.

claim: The LINCS L1000 data are produced with methods representative of DGI research and free from social, prior knowledge and narrow methodological dependencies associated with the sequential publication of findings by communities of researchers.
source: Rather, we argue that the LINCS L1000 data are: i) produced with methods representative of DGI research; ii) free from social, prior knowledge and narrow methodological dependencies associated with the sequential publication of findings by communities of researchers.
evidence: This is an argument about the advantages of using LINCS L1000 data for replication assessment.

claim: The manuscript attempts to elucidate biases introduced by the social, cultural and methodological structure of science to noisy experimental data.
source: In this way, our manuscript attempts to elucidate biases introduced by the social, cultural and methodological structure of science to noisy experimental data.
evidence: This is a statement about the goal of the paper.

claim: LINCS L1000 experiments must remain unfiltered by the publication system and the expectations of any particular scientific community.
source: From this perspective, LINCS L1000 experiments must remain unfiltered by the publication system and the expectations of any particular scientific community.
evidence: This is an argument about the importance of using unfiltered high-throughput data.

claim: In the current state of the biomedical literature, where most reported results are confirmatory, scalable approaches for identifying uncertain claims are in short supply.
source: In the current state of the biomedical literature, where most reported results are confirmatory, scalable approaches for identifying uncertain claims are in short supply.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this paper addresses.

claim: Experimental data such as the LINCS L1000 provides an informed approach to evaluate published claims.
source: Experimental data such as the LINCS L1000 provides an informed approach to evaluate published claims.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the value of high-throughput data for replication assessment.

claim: With the proliferation of high-throughput experimental platforms and improvements in cross-platform reproducibility, the approach reported here could be further refined and extended to a continuous replication system that revises scientific results in light of new experimental evidence.
source: With the proliferation of high-throughput experimental platforms and improvements in cross-platform reproducibility (Haibe-Kains et al., 2013), the approach we report here could be further refined and extended to a continuous replication system (Goodman et al., 2016) that revises scientific results in light of new experimental evidence, increasing the credibility and robustness of biomedical knowledge.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the approach, supported by citations.

claim: The analysis represents the largest biomedical replication of its kind to date.
source: Despite the smaller size of this subsample, our analysis represents the largest biomedical replication of its kind to date.
evidence: This is a claim about the scale of the analysis compared to prior work.

claim: The data and computer code associated with this analysis are available on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/xmvda/.
source: The data and computer code associated with this analysis are available on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/xmvda/.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.
